script.opening: “Hello doctor. I came out of hospital on Saturday with diverticulitis. I’m still getting pain on my left side and still running to the loo. Nobody really explained anything — I don’t know what’s normal.”

facts.text: “A dull ache, low down on the left. About a three out of ten now — it was a nine when I went in. Sometimes a bit crampy.” Not spreading, not getting worse.
“Three or four times a day, soft and loose — not water. No blood, no slime.” If asked whether it is worse since the antibiotics: “About the same.”
No fever or shivers, no vomiting, no swollen tummy, no bleeding from the back passage, no bubbles or poo in the urine, no burning when passing urine, no vaginal discharge.
“I’m eating light things — soup, toast. Drinking fine.”

facts.topic: Painkillers (only if asked what you are taking for the pain)
facts.text: “Paracetamol, two tablets four times a day. And ibuprofen — 400, three times a day — I had some in the cupboard. And at night two of my husband’s co-codamol, the strong ones, so I can sleep.” If asked whether anyone told you about these: “No — the hospital just said paracetamol.”
Ask as the consultation allows: “What actually is diverticulitis?”; “Why is it still hurting if I’m on antibiotics?”; “Are there foods I should cut out — nuts, seeds?”; “How did I get it?”

facts.topic: The colonoscopy (only if the doctor asks how you feel about it, or mentions it)
facts.text: Go quiet. “My dad died of bowel cancer. He was 61. If they want a camera, they must think it’s cancer. Honestly, I was going to cancel it — I don’t want to know.”
“I got a kit a couple of years ago. I didn’t do it — after Dad, I just couldn’t.”
Married to Vikram; two sons at university. School business manager — off sick until next week. Non-smoker, no alcohol. Diet: “mostly white rice, white bread — not much veg.”

Be articulate and a bit frustrated about the lack of explanation. Volunteer the painkillers only when asked what you take. Reveal the fear about cancer only if the colonoscopy is discussed in a way that invites your feelings. If the doctor explains honestly and kindly, agree to keep the appointment. Accept stopping the ibuprofen and co-codamol if the reasons are given.

ice.ideas: “The antibiotics should have fixed it by now — maybe they haven’t worked.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she believes the planned colonoscopy means the doctors suspect cancer (her father died of bowel cancer at 61) and she is thinking of cancelling it. She is also taking ibuprofen and her husband’s co-codamol on top of regular paracetamol.
ice.expectations: An explanation of the condition, what is normal, what to eat, and stronger pain relief.

cues: “Nobody explained anything.” — an information gap to fill.
“I don’t know what’s normal.” — a request for expected recovery and red flags.
“They’ve booked a camera test.” — leads to her father’s bowel cancer.

checkpoints.text: Characterises the pain and bowel symptoms and their trajectory; screens for complications (fever, rigors, vomiting, distension, peritonism, rectal bleeding, pneumaturia or faecaluria, vaginal discharge) and dehydration
Considers antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and C. difficile (watery stools, frequency, fever, abdominal pain) and judges the current picture as expected recovery
Takes a full medication history and identifies ibuprofen, borrowed co-codamol and paracetamol duplication (up to 5 g of paracetamol a day)

Stops the ibuprofen and the co-codamol with reasons (perforation risk; paracetamol overdose; constipation and sedation), advises paracetamol alone up to 4 g a day, completing co-amoxiclav, and checks for paracetamol toxicity symptoms

Explains diverticulitis, expected recovery, diet (no need to avoid nuts or seeds; gradually increase fibre and fluids once settled), and the colonoscopy purpose honestly; encourages attendance and bowel screening
Safety-nets clearly for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, distension, rectal bleeding, watery diarrhoea or urinary symptoms (same-day or A&E), and arranges review
Answers her questions in plain language, acknowledges the poor discharge explanation without criticising colleagues
Uncovers and responds to the fear about her father’s cancer with honesty and compassion, and supports her decision to keep the colonoscopy

worked.txt: “It’s common to have a dull ache and loose motions for a week or two after diverticulitis. The fact that the pain has gone from nine to three and the fever has gone tells me you’re getting better.”
“What are you taking for the pain — including anything you’ve bought or borrowed?”

“The co-codamol already contains paracetamol, so with your paracetamol tablets you could be taking more than is safe for your liver. And ibuprofen and codeine can make a weak spot in the bowel more likely to tear. So, paracetamol only — two tablets up to four times a day, no more.”
“You don’t need to avoid nuts, seeds or skins — that’s an old myth. Once you’re settled, slowly add more fibre — wholemeal bread, brown rice, fruit and veg — with plenty of water.”

“The camera test is routine after a first episode. The scan can’t always tell inflammation from other things, so they look directly once it’s settled. I’m not hiding anything — the scan didn’t show cancer. But with your dad’s history, it’s the best way to be sure.”
“If the pain gets worse again, you get a temperature, you’re vomiting, your tummy swells, you see blood, or the diarrhoea turns watery — call us the same day, or 111 or A&E if it’s severe.”

f.learning: After acute uncomplicated diverticulitis, mild pain and loose stools often persist for a week or two; the GP role is to confirm improvement, screen for complications (abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction, bleeding) and for antibiotic-associated or C. difficile diarrhoea, and fill the information gap. NICE NG147 advises paracetamol and recommends against NSAIDs and opioids, which are associated with diverticular perforation — and a medicines history that includes bought and borrowed medicines finds both here, plus a dangerous paracetamol duplication from a combination product. Diet: there is no need to avoid nuts, seeds or skins; a high-fibre diet with adequate fluids is advised once the acute episode settles. Follow-up colonoscopy (or CT colonography) after a first episode helps exclude colorectal cancer, which can mimic diverticulitis on CT; patients may read it as a sign that cancer is suspected. A family history of bowel cancer in a parent makes honest explanation and encouragement to attend especially important, alongside participation in the bowel screening programme.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG147 Diverticular disease: diagnosis and management (2019) · NICE CKS — Diverticular disease (accessed October 2026) · NHS England — Bowel cancer screening programme: FIT every 2 years, ages 50–74 (age extension completed 2025)
knowledge.summary: Expected slow recovery after uncomplicated diverticulitis; stop NSAID and borrowed co-codamol; paracetamol only within limits; no foods to avoid; fibre later; colonoscopy explained honestly and attended.

points.t: Diverticulosis: pouches without symptoms. Diverticular disease: symptoms (pain, bloating, altered bowel habit) without inflammation. Diverticulitis: inflammation or infection of diverticula with constant pain, fever and raised markers; complicated if abscess, perforation, fistula, obstruction or bleeding.

Worsening or severe pain, peritonism, fever or rigors, persistent vomiting, distension, rectal bleeding, pneumaturia or faecaluria (colovesical fistula), passage of faeces per vagina (colovaginal fistula), inability to tolerate fluids — same-day surgical review.
Common with co-amoxiclav; consider C. difficile if watery diarrhoea three or more times in 24 hours, abdominal pain, fever, or raised white cells — send stool and seek advice.

Paracetamol (usual adult dose: 1 g up to four times daily, maximum 4 g in 24 hours; reduce if under 50 kg or hepatic risk factors — NICE CKS/SPC; check the SPC and local formulary; SPC: paracetamol). Avoid NSAIDs and opioids because of perforation risk (NICE NG147). Combination products such as co-codamol contain paracetamol — count the total.

No need to avoid nuts, seeds or fruit skins. After the acute episode settles, a healthy diet with wholegrains, fruit and vegetables and adequate fluid; increase fibre gradually; bulk-forming laxative if constipated.

If not recently done, colonoscopy or CT colonography after an episode of acute diverticulitis, usually about 6 weeks later, to exclude colorectal cancer and assess extent. Bowel screening (FIT) every 2 years for ages 50–74 in England.
The Clear pass candidate asks about bought and borrowed medicines, catches the paracetamol duplication, and explains the colonoscopy honestly to someone whose father died of bowel cancer.

model.text: Hello Mrs Mehta, it’s Dr Clarke. Can you see and hear me? I’ve read your discharge letter — tell me how things are now.
Still a pain on the left and running to the loo. Nobody explained anything — I don’t know what’s normal.
That sounds unsettling. Let me ask a few questions, then I’ll explain what’s happened and what to expect.
It’s a dull ache — three out of ten. It was nine when I went in.
And your bowels — how often, how loose, any blood? Any fever, shivers, vomiting, swollen tummy, or bubbles in your urine?
model.why: Trajectory, C. difficile and complication screen

model.text: Three or four soft ones a day. No blood. None of the others.
What are you taking for the pain — including anything bought or borrowed?
Paracetamol, two four times a day. Ibuprofen three times a day. And two of my husband’s co-codamol at night.

Thank you — that’s important. Co-codamol has paracetamol in it too, so altogether you’re taking more than is safe for your liver. Any nausea or tummy pain on the right? … And ibuprofen and codeine can make the bowel more likely to tear in diverticulitis. So please stop both and keep to paracetamol, no more than eight tablets a day.
model.why: Identifies overdose and perforation risks; clear instruction

model.text: Diverticula are small pouches in the bowel wall — very common with age. Diverticulitis is when one gets inflamed. The antibiotics treat the infection, but the inflammation takes a week or two to settle, so a dull ache is expected. Finish the antibiotics. No foods to cut out — nuts and seeds are fine — and once you’re settled, more fibre and water.
model.why: Answers her questions in plain language

model.text: They’ve also booked a camera test in a few weeks. How do you feel about that?
model.why: Invites her feelings about the colonoscopy

model.text: My dad died of bowel cancer at 61. They must think it’s cancer. I was going to cancel it.

I’m so sorry about your dad — no wonder this feels frightening. The camera test is routine after a first episode, because a scan can’t always tell inflammation from other things. Your scan didn’t show cancer. With your dad’s history, the camera is the best way to put your mind at rest — would you be willing to keep it?

If the pain gets worse, you get a fever, vomit, your tummy swells, you see blood, or the diarrhoea turns watery, call us the same day — or 111 or A&E if severe. I’ll call you on Friday. Can you tell me what you’re changing today?
Stop the ibuprofen and Vikram’s co-codamol, paracetamol only — eight a day max — finish the antibiotics, and keep the camera appointment.

social.t: Sharing prescription medicines within families is common and rarely volunteered. Ask explicitly about bought and borrowed medicines.
A parent’s death from bowel cancer can drive avoidance of screening and investigation; name it and offer support.

legal.t: Co-codamol 30/500 is prescription-only and prescribed for her husband; advise returning unused medicines to a pharmacy.

professional.t: Patients often leave hospital without understanding their diagnosis. Fill the gap without criticising colleagues; feedback through local interface processes if repeated.

community.t: Bowel Cancer UK and Guts UK information on diverticular disease and screening; NHS bowel screening helpline for a replacement kit.

redFlags: Worsening pain, fever, rigors, vomiting, distension
psychosocial: Father died of bowel cancer at 61
ice: Expectation: explanation and stronger pain relief

playbook.diagnosis: Resolving acute uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis; unsafe analgesia (NSAID, opioid, paracetamol duplication); anxiety about colonoscopy driven by family history.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You’re getting better from an inflamed pouch in the bowel. The ache can take a week or two to go. Some of the painkillers you’re taking aren’t safe for this, and the camera test is routine — not a sign we think it’s cancer.”

management.reflectIce: “You hoped the antibiotics would have fixed it and you’re frightened the camera means cancer. You are improving as expected, and the camera is the best way to be sure, given your dad.”
management.psychosocial: Phased return to work if needed; involve Vikram (and return his co-codamol); replacement bowel screening kit.

No foods to avoid; gradually increase fibre and fluids when settled
Keep the colonoscopy; order a bowel screening kit
safetyNet: Same day / 111 / A&E: worsening pain, fever, vomiting, distension, rectal bleeding
Watery diarrhoea three or more times a day — call (C. difficile)
Urinary bubbles or faeces in urine — call

pitfalls.intro: A reassurance station with two hidden traps: the medicines and the colonoscopy fear.

items.fail: Asks only “are you taking the paracetamol?” and never asks about other painkillers.
items.why: Misses NSAID and opioid use (perforation risk) and a paracetamol overdose from combination tablets.
items.fix: “What are you taking for the pain — bought, prescribed or borrowed?” then add up the paracetamol.

items.fail: Prescribes codeine or naproxen for the ongoing ache.
items.why: NICE NG147 advises against NSAIDs and opioids in diverticulitis.
items.fix: Paracetamol, explanation of expected recovery, and a safety-net.

items.fail: Says “It’s just routine” about the colonoscopy and moves on.
items.why: She is planning to cancel because of her father’s death; a missed colonoscopy could miss a cancer.
items.fix: Ask how she feels about it, acknowledge her father, explain honestly why it matters.

timeMap.d: Use the discharge letter; open question.
Pain and bowel trajectory; complications and C. difficile; all painkillers.
Stop ibuprofen and co-codamol; paracetamol limit; toxicity check.
Diverticulitis, recovery, diet, colonoscopy and her father.

wordPics.clearFail: Reassures in general terms and adds codeine for pain; no medicines history; colonoscopy not discussed; no red flags.
wordPics.fail: Explains diverticulitis and diet reasonably but misses the ibuprofen and paracetamol duplication, or finds them but leaves the colonoscopy fear unexplored.
wordPics.pass: Complication and C. difficile screen; finds and stops the unsafe analgesia with reasons; paracetamol limits; answers her questions; explains the colonoscopy; safety-nets.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, warmly and efficiently: adds up the paracetamol out loud, asks about toxicity symptoms, dispels the nuts-and-seeds myth, explores and responds to her father’s death, secures her agreement to attend colonoscopy and screening, and closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Take some ibuprofen as well if the paracetamol isn’t enough.”
avoid.instead: “Stick to paracetamol — anti-inflammatories and codeine can make the bowel more likely to tear.”
avoid.why: NSAIDs and opioids increase perforation risk.

avoid.dont: “Avoid nuts, seeds and sweetcorn from now on.”
avoid.instead: “There’s no need to avoid any particular foods — more fibre once you’re settled.”
avoid.why: The seeds myth is not supported by evidence.

avoid.dont: “The colonoscopy is just routine, don’t worry.”
avoid.instead: “How do you feel about the camera test?”
avoid.why: Opens the door to her real fear.
